item.title: PSG’s Luis Enrique Hopes Man City Avoids Sanctions After Financial Rules Verdict
item.description: Paris Saint-Germain coach Luis Enrique has come to Manchester City’s defense, saying he hopes the club won’t be stripped of titles after being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.
item.content:encoded: Paris Saint-Germain coach Luis Enrique came to Manchester City's defense on Tuesday, saying he hopes the club won't be stripped of titles after being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. Back-to-back Champions League winner PSG plays City at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday. City could face sanctions including a huge fine, points deductions or even expulsion from England's top flight. There have also been calls for it to be stripped of trophies it won during a nine-year period in which it was found to have artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1 billion. "I hope everything works out well for Man City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible over the last few years and they certainly deserved to win all the trophies they have won," Luis Enrique said ahead of the Champions League game. "The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction. "But now we have to wait to see what the authorities decide or the judge is going to say." City is under Abu Dhabi ownership and PSG is Qatari-backed. Both clubs have been sanctioned by European governing body UEFA for breaching Financial Fair Play regulations in the past. City is accused of providing misleading information about its finances from 2009-18. During that time, it won three titles. It has appealed the verdict. City defender Ruben Dias said the players were focusing on the pitch, like they did Sunday in a 3-0 win over Liverpool at Anfield. "I feel like when you build yourself as a player, you build yourself against any kind of noise," he said. "Personally, and I really feel like I speak for the whole group, we’re very calm. We trust the club, we’re very calm and we’re very focused on enjoying football." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: World Soccer Rankings: Why Manchester City Is Ahead Of Barcelona, For Now
item.description: Ranking the top-20 club teams in world soccer seven weeks into new the season.
item.content:encoded: With FIFA's extended 16-day international break over, club soccer roared back to the forefront over the weekend. The action didn't disappoint, especially in Europe, where some of the game's biggest teams and players wowed fans before the spotlight shifts to a full slate of UEFA Champions League matches midweek. Before those matches kick off, here's where the world's best clubs rank seven weeks into the 2026-27 season: Now 3-1-1 after Saturday’s stirring 4-3 triumph away to Mainz, Leverkusen is all alone in 4th in the Bundesliga. Life is good on the blue side of Rome, with Lazio still unbeaten (4-0-1) and even on points with Serie A leaders and Scudetto holders Inter. Like Brighton, Brentford is what the standings say they are: a Champions League qualifier on goal difference if the Premier League season ended today. It’s hard to argue with an 8-0 record, which is what Porto has in Liga Portugal so far. They’ll go for a first Champions League win on Wednesday, across the Spanish border against Betis. The Reds' reputation precedes them, which is why the 2025 Premier League champs are here despite a slow start to life under new Spanish boss Andoni Iraola. With just two wins from six played following Sunday’s lopsided loss to City, Liverpool is ninth in the Prem. They’ll need to rebound next weekend at fourth-place Brentford, but first must travel to Austria for a midweek Champions League date with LASK. Monaco has rebounded from finishing seventh in France’s top flight last season to leading Ligue 1 six games into 2026-27. And they’ve done it mostly without U.S. World Cup star Folarin Balogun, who has logged just 46 minutes since missing four matches immediately before and after his transfer deadline day move to Everton collapsed at the 11th hour. Last season, Roma finished in Italy’s Top 3 for the first time in seven years. The Giallorossi occupy the same spot more than six weeks into the new Serie A campaign. Yet maintaining that position will depend on how well Paulo Dybala and his teammates manage fighting on multiple fronts; Roma hosts Real Mardid in Champions League action on Wednesday. The Blues look good under first-year manager Xabi Alonso, who oversaw Chelsea’s biggest win of the season on Saturday, a 5-1 smackdown of usually plucky Bournemouth. Led by English playmakers Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers and Brazilian striker João Pedro, the London club is well-positioned to compete for a top 3 finish for the first time since 2021-22. In fairness, Freiburg probably could be even higher on this list. It’s no accident that they’re leading the Bundesliga ahead of both Dortmund and Bayern five matches in. The "Breisgau Brazilians" stayed unbeaten on Sunday despite playing the final 26 minutes of their 2-1 win over Schalke with 10 men. Real Betis is even on points in La Liga with second-place Atleti and one clear of Real Madrid in fourth, with a 6-1-1 record so far. They trounced Osasuna 5-2 on Sunday. Is Betis the real deal? We’ll find out as soon as Saturday, when the Heliopolitanos welcome table-topping Barcelona to Estadio La Cartuja in Seville. Given the hardware-laden history of some of the names on this list, Brighton looks like an outlier. But there’s no arguing with the Seagulls’ results in the notoriously unforgiving Premier League. With four wins and a tie in its first six outings, including that eyebrow-raising demolition of Arsenal, BHA is deservedly all alone in third place — ahead of regular top-six contenders like Aston Villa, Chelsea, Liverpool, Manchester United, Newcastle and Tottenham. With 15 European titles, global soccer’s most decorated club team has more than twice as many as any of its competitors. It’s therefore jarring to see Real clinging to the final Champions League berth in Spain, or way back in 13th place in the current league phase standings. At least the latter is deceptive: José Mourinho’s side opened this season’s European slate with a hard-fought 2-1 win over Inter. They’ll visit Roma on Wednesday, but Los Blancos' biggest test this month is its six-pointer with La Liga-leading Barcelona on Oct. 25. Despite reaching the Champions League final in 2024, the Black & Yellow’s most famous achievement over the last few years has been producing global superstars Jude Bellingham and Erling Haaland before selling them to Real Madrid and Manchester City, respectively. But BVB is currently tied with Freiburg for the most points in the Bundesliga — Dortmund last won the German title in 2012 — and two points clear of mighty Bayern, which they’ll visit on Halloween. Spain’s second-place team is a point clear of its cross-capital rivals Real Madrid — which it beat 2-1 on Sept. 20 — after eight La Liga games. Diego Simeone has just two losses across all competitions so far, one in its Champions League opener in Liverpool. Atléti hosts Manchester United on Tuesday in its second match of the league phase. With three Serie A titles in the last six seasons, Inter has been Italy’s most dominant squad this decade. Led by Argentine striker Lauturo Martinez, the European silver medalists in 2023 and 2025 are again leading the race for the Scudetto six games into the current term. The host start could continue. The Nerazzurri play three of their next four games at the San Siro, including winnable Champions League matches this month against Belgium’s Club Brugge and Ukraine’s Shakhtar Donetsk. The championship hangover has been real the second time around for the Parisians, who sit sixth in Ligue 1 after six games and wouldn’t even qualify for Europe’s top club competition if the French season ended today. They’ve still lost just once, narrowly, to league-leading Monaco early last month. Upcoming tests against Man City (on Wednesday) and Barcelona (Oct. 20) will reveal plenty about how seriously PSG will contend for a third consecutive Champions League crown. Although Harry Kane & Co. sit atop the respected Elo club rankings ahead of Arsenal and City, they’re languishing in third in Germany after five games played Bundesliga. The standings are disorienting for a club that has hoisted the silverware in 13 of the last 14 seasons, including 2025-26. Bayern has scored four or more goals in four of its last seven matches. Shooting for its first Champions League title since 2020, "FC Hollywood" next heads to the Norwegian city of Stavanger to take on Viking on Tuesday. Despite a shocking 3-0 loss to Brighton just before the international break began, last year’s Premier League winners and European runners-up remain near the very top of the club game. The Gunners have won the other six matches they’ve played, including Saturday’s gritty, 2-1, come-from-behind victory over Leeds in North London. They topped Napoli in Italy last month, keeping a clean sheet, and should contend for both the English and Champions League honors again in 2026-27. After losing the final to PSG on penalties last term, Arsenal’s Oct. 21 trip to German titans Bayern will be telling. Led by newly minted teenage World Cup winners Pau Cubarsí and Lamine Yamal and 30-year-old Golden Ball recipient Rodri — whom Barça signed from Manchester City following Spain’s mid-July triumph in New Jersey — the Blaugrana have started their La Liga title defense 8-0. Only goal difference separates them from PSG and Bayern Munich atop the Champions League table; Barcelona, which travels to Turkey to face Galatasaray on Tuesday, thumped Dutch power Feyenoord 5-1 in its opener. It feels wrong to have Man City atop this list given the financial scandal that has engulfed the Abu Dhabi-backed club in recent weeks. But hey, (alleged) cheating works. While it remains to be seen if the Sky Blues will even remain in the Premier League if they lose the case again on appeal, Sunday’s 3-0 demolition of Liverpool at Anfield confirmed that City, now a perfect 6-0 to start the new Prem season, is the best team in the best domestic circuit in the world. Enzo Maresca’s side also opened their UEFA Champions League campaign last month with a 2-0 victory away to Porto. The Cityzens host two-time defending European titlists Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday in one of the marquee contests of the first round.

item.title: How Emma Hayes Is Changing The USWNT And Transforming The Women's Game
item.description: USWNT manager Emma Hayes is instilling a vision that considers every aspect of the female player’s experience on and off the field.
item.content:encoded: U.S. NATIONAL TEAM TRAINING CENTER (Fayetteville, Ga.) – The epiphany came to Emma Hayes about a decade ago. She was well into her coaching tenure at Chelsea and her team had just lost to rivals Arsenal, 1-0, in the 2016 FA Cup final at Wembley Stadium. When Hayes talks about this moment, she explains the Gunners deserved to win that game. What she couldn’t see at the time – but very clearly understands now – is why her players were so off that day. Their reaction times were slower than normal and their coordination was like "watching a group of people that looked separated from their bodies," Hayes recently told a small group of reporters at the U.S. Soccer National Training Center near Atlanta. "I remember in the middle of the game thinking, ‘What’s wrong with them?’" Hayes continued. "‘Is it their nerves?’" Hayes later learned her players were at different points in their menstrual cycles and that, in some cases, those hormonal fluctuations were affecting their performance. She was at a loss. "Why don’t I know these things?" she asked herself. Brain fog, fluid retention, inflammation, cramping, pelvic floor issues – these are things women know all too well. This caused Hayes to think about her own body – she’s been open about her endometriosis diagnosis – and how little she really knew. In her players’ case, they were navigating this while trying to compete at the highest level. "We’re asking players to perform in a culture that says, ‘Oh, you’ve got a period? Sit out,’" Hayes said. "I was like, ‘It’s not good enough. We don’t want to sit out." Since then, Hayes has made it her life’s work to normalize conversations around women’s health and transform what was once treated as a taboo topic into a superpower. Through her own research, she discovered there is no degree devoted solely on female physiology. If she wanted to truly understand women’s bodies, she would have to build that education herself – seeking out scientists, former players, coaches and other like-minded people who were asking the same questions. So she did. The result is an entire ecosystem – first at Chelsea and now as the U.S. women’s national team manager – created around putting the female lens "at the heart of everything we do." Part of the end goal is that this contributes to developing a team to win. The Americans are preparing for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and then the Olympics on home soil in 2028. The squad is currently in the middle of an international window – they fell to Spain 2-0 in a friendly on Saturday and will face the defending World Cup champions again on Tuesday – before turning focus to qualifying for next summer’s tournament in November. The other part, though, is larger than that. Hayes and her passionate staff want to share their findings with women and girls at every level of the sport. Which is why Hayes and U.S. Soccer opened the second annual HerLens Conference – which was held internally last year – to 300 people, ranging from NWSL general managers to youth soccer coaches at the National Training Center earlier this month. The two-day event included interactive sessions about bias and inclusivity, why girls stay or leave the game, building women- and girls-centric team culture, and more. And she introduced attendees to the term "Female 360," a holistic approach that considers every aspect of the female player’s experience on and off the field. "For me, this is more than winning on the pitch," Hayes said. "This is transformational. I think my purpose, my mission, came from a losing situation and I felt robbed. I felt denied. I felt like, how have I, at this stage of my life, [not known] these things about myself?" HAYES TOOK OVER as the U.S. national team head coach a few weeks before the 2024 Paris Olympics. It was a whirlwind way to begin a new job, and she led a group of players she’d only just met to a gold medal. Afterward, she surveyed every player and staff member: "OK, where do we go from here?" A couple of months later, Hayes introduced her approach for reframing women’s soccer through a female lens in an effort to not just copy and paste a game inherited from men. She’s been instilling her vision ever since. "It was like a light bulb went off in my brain, like, ‘Yeah, duh!’" U.S. and Manchester City midfielder Sam Coffey told me. "It was like, ‘Wow, this makes so much sense. How am I just recognizing this?’ It was almost like catching my own bias and my own acceptance for how things had been up until that point." A fundamental part of Hayes’ methodology is the recognition that women and men have distinct needs, from nutrition, sleep and recovery to uniforms and even the placement of scales outside the locker room. Her staff has examined data revealing differences in how male and female players cross the ball into the box and how much space goalkeepers take up within it. What works for men doesn’t necessarily work for women, and building a better blueprint starts with understanding those differences. "I think so much of the women's game has just been dominated by what we know to be true of male players instead of, hang on a second, these are completely different athletes," said Coffey, who was part of the squad that won Olympic gold two years ago. "And that’s not a weakness or a disadvantage. It’s just, how do we best serve us instead of how do you get the best out of men. Because we’re not men." Hayes calls the senior team her "proving lab" and the National Training Center serves as an incubator for new ideas – a space to think critically, connect and reimagine what’s possible. The goal is for those principles to extend beyond the national team, reaching youth clubs and soccer communities across the country. With support from the federation and its CEO and secretary general JT Batson, Hayes hopes to transform the future of the game for women and girls. The 2031 World Cup, which the U.S. plans to co-host, offers a chance to see how much progress can be made when the needs of female athletes are at the center of the conversation. "Emma wants us to be trendsetters," Tash Patel, director of sporting analytics for the women’s national team, said during her classroom session about coaching the women’s game. That’s what this program has always been known for. From winning World Cups to finding ways to start families while continuing to play to fighting for equal pay, the national team has consistently pushed the game forward, striving to leave it better than they found it and serve as role models around the world. This is simply the next iteration of that legacy. THE IMPACT THIS has had on the players has been transformative. Hayes has seen their confidence grow as they’ve gained more knowledge, and Coffey can attest to this. She’s more comfortable speaking openly about where she is in her cycle and how her body feels, whether she’s competing for club or country. Georgie Bruinvels, the female health and research innovation lead for the team, has played an integral role in spearheading much of this. She tracks the players’ cycles and Oura Ring stats – only if they are willing as this is not mandatory – to better understand each player’s individual needs and how to best support them. "She’s always looking for little 1% ways to approach things from a female point of view, down to the temperature of our meeting room," Coffey said, noting that it should be 68 degrees because that’s the temperature that women process information most efficiently. "I’ll be filling my plate for dinner and she’s like, ‘I would get extra anti-inflammatory foods if I were you!’ And I'm like, ‘All I want is chocolate, but OK!’" Coffey said, laughing. "All these little things add up over time and cumulatively make such an impact on how we feel and how we perform. "They’re detailed down to the T. It’s not just taking an ibuprofen and calling it a day. And I've noticed a difference." As for how this entire mindset is spreading across the sport, Coffey said she brings back habits from national team camp to Man City – like the "yogurt pot" parfait recipe that Bruinvels has introduced her to. "In my club and country environments, I do 100% feel like nothing is a hand-me-down," Coffey said. "It feels tailored to being a female and we’re only going deeper in our understanding of that, which is super cool." While Hayes’ strategy may end up giving the Americans a competitive edge – because not every team or federation will have these same resources – all of this information is not something they plan to gatekeep. "I want every little girl and woman, no matter what your practice is in our sport, to feel like this is more than just playing the game," Hayes said. "I think we can impact society in a profound way."

item.title: Lionel Messi Scores Twice For Inter Miami In 1st Game Since Argentina Retirement
item.description: Lionel Messi scored two goals to give him a league-leading 23 this season, and Inter Miami beat D.C. United 4-0 on Saturday night.
item.content:encoded: Lionel Messi scored two goals to give him a league-leading 23 this season, and Inter Miami beat D.C. United 4-0 on Saturday night. Luis Suarez also scored twice and German Berterame had two assists for Inter Miami, which snapped a five-match winless skid. Miami had four draws and one loss before Saturday’s outburst. Four days after playing his farewell match that ended a 21-year tenure with the Argentine national team, Messi played the entire 90 minutes. The win was Miami’s first since a 7-1 rout of CF Montreal on Aug. 29. It was also the first league win for new coach Cristian "Kily" González, who took over Sept. 16. D.C. United is winless in its last five matches. Messi scored his first in the 47th minute after Suárez tallied twice in the first half to give Inter Miami a 2-0 lead at the break. Suárez centered a pass near the 6-yard box, where Messi retrieved it and tapped in a shot inside the right post. Inter Miami padded its lead when Messi struck again in the 60th minute. He received Rodrigo De Paul’s pass, dribbled inside the large area and eluded two United defenders to beat goalkeeper Sean Johnson with a shot from 12 yards. Inter Miami’s first scoring threat resulted in Suárez’s goal three minutes into the match. Suárez received Berterame’s header and beat Johnson with a shot that landed inside the left post. Suárez made it 2-0 with his second goal in the 39th minute. Johnson deflected Messi’s point-blank shot to an open Berterame, who fed Suárez with another header that he retrieved inside the 6-yard box. Suárez then tapped in a shot for his brace. Up next Inter Miami hosts New York City FC on Wednesday night. D.C. United faces the New York Red Bulls on Wednesday night. Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: Alexi Lalas' Post-World Cup Power Rankings: France Or Spain At The Top?
item.description: FOX Soccer analyst Alexi Lalas ranks and explains his top ten soccer squads in the world.
item.content:encoded: This is my first post-World Cup power rankings. I love power rankings and I especially love counter rankings. FIFA has their own rankings (released on Oct. 7), and I'm sure they spend a lot of time and money and technology on the formula to come up with it. I can't say I do the same, it's more of a gut feel. But these are my power rankings, and as I have always said: If you don't like mine, then get your own. FIFA rank: 11 2026 World Cup Recap: A lot of expectations this summer were put on the Colombians, who were among the trendy dark-horse contenders to win it all. Luis Diaz, who has shined as an attacker for Liverpool and now Bayern Munich, balanced out a tough defense. Nevertheless, a round of 16 loss to an equally stout Switzerland side ended the dream. What's Happened Since: The Colombians had a relatively uneventful window with a win (over Peru), a loss (to Paraguay), and a draw with Mexico (who is ranked No. 10 by FIFA instead) in friendly competition. But Los Cafeteros could make an argument about now being South America's toughest side. Next Opponents: TBD Alexi's Take: "FIFA has Mexico at this spot, but I just think that's ridiculous." FIFA rank: 6 2026 World Cup Recap: History was made in 2022 as Morocco became the first African nation to reach a men's World Cup semifinals. Leaning on talent that grew up playing in leagues across Europe, Morocco has become a machine. The Atlas Lions lost to France in the quarterfinals (having lost to them in the 2022 semis), but its young core and success at youth tournament levels will keep them around. What's Happened Since: Morocco cruised to two wins in 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying in September. The drama surrounding the team will be off the pitch as a court ruling this month will decide whether Morocco or Senegal will ultimately be named AFCON champions following the controversial final in 2025. Next Opponents: TBD Alexi's Take: "After making the 2022 World Cup semifinals, we were interested to see whether they could continue that momentum in 2026. Whether it was just a Golden Generation, or it was a moment in time and would be a Croatia-esque storyarc. I think Morocco and this generation of players have proved they are here to stay." FIFA rank: 9 2026 World Cup Recap: The team that has historically been among the world's elite (three times runner-up at the men's tournament) provided plenty of entertaining football, backed by one of the best fanbases out there. In the attack, Cody Gakpo and Brian Brobbey shined while the ageless Virgil van Dijk remained the heart-and-soul in defense. A tough loss in the round of 32 against Morocco ended the Oranje's tournament. What's Happened Since: Xavi Hernandez, one of the greatest midfielders in Barcelona history and a 2010 World Cup winner with Spain, was surprisingly picked to be the Netherlands' new manager. Two wins over Serbia and two draws (vs. Germany and Greece) in Nations League action got the Xavi era started on the right foot. Next Opponents: vs. Greece (Nov. 13); vs. Germany (Nov. 16) Alexi's Take: "The Dutch have still never ultimately won the World Cup, but they are still a good solid team. I can be convinced otherwise, but I'm going to give them the benefit of the doubt." FIFA rank: 8 2026 World Cup Recap: It initially felt like its Golden Generation players of striker Romelu Lukaku, midfielder Kevin De Bruyne, and goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois wouldn't be able to compete at this tournament. But the Red Devils proved people wrong, especially the U.S. men's national team. After a 4-1 beatdown over the USMNT in the round of 16, they would lose to Spain in the quarterfinals. What's Happened Since: Two losses to a more talented France team in the Nations League during this recent window should be tempered by wins over Italy and Türkiye. Those Golden Generation veterans will certainly now give way as talents like winger Jérémy Doku are emerging. Next Opponents: vs. Türkiye (Nov. 12); vs. Italy (Nov. 15) Alexi's Take: "Speaking of good solid teams, we have Belgium next. The U.S. found out in the worst possible way and at the worst possible time how good this team can be." FIFA rank: 5 2026 World Cup Recap: This team was still one of the biggest draws at the tournament, but the product on the field (led by star winger Vinícius Jr.) never lived up to those mythical yellow jerseys. It's now 24 years since Brazil's last World Cup title. Carlo Ancelotti, one of Europe's greatest club managers at places like Real Madrid and AC Milan, came in to lead a team chock-full of individual talent. Nonetheless, the Seleçao bowed out to Norway in the round of 16. What's Happened Since: Ancelotti remains, Vinicius has had some struggles with his club Real Madrid, and there are still questions about who'll be the next generation's stars. Three wins in friendlies (two against Australia, one against India) aren't going to clarify issues in key areas like defense. Next Opponents: TBD Alexi's Take: "I was high on Brazil, and they did nothing to change that during the World Cup. It's still Brazil, there is still an element of Germany where they are constantly hanging on to the fact." FIFA rank: 2 2026 World Cup Recap: It was going to be Lionel Messi's Last Dance on the international stage, and Argentina nearly pulled it off. After winning it all in 2022, La Albiceleste reached the final in the summer but was dominated by Spain in a tough 1-0 loss. Even at age 39, Messi was the focal point and the inspirational guiding light for a talented team. He finished with 8 goals, behind only France's Kylian Mbappé in the Golden Boot race. What's Happened Since: Messi officially bid adios to playing for Argentina in a send-off match against African team Benin. It was an emotional night on Oct. 6 in Buenos Aires as a whole nation honored one of sport's greatest figures. The era changes, but the talent will still be there with youngsters like Julian Alvarez, Enzo Fernández and Nico Paz leading the team. Next Opponents: TBD Alexi's Take: "Most people have Argentina in the top 2, including FIFA, but I'm putting them here. Going to back-to-back World Cup finals and winning in 2022 is impressive, but this is an Argentina team that is now playing without their most important player. Let's be honest, they rode Messi, and he carried them in many ways. They did it willingly and were a wonderful team to watch and obviously incredibly successful. Now we don't know what this team is going to look like going forward without Messi. We have seen Argentina play without Messi, and they have plenty of talent and will continue to be a top-10 team. But it's a changing of a specific guard here – it's not even a change because there's nobody who could ever replace him." FIFA rank: 7 2026 World Cup Recap: Aside from a 5-0 win over debut team Uzbekistan in the group stage, Cristiano Ronaldo and Co. never lived up to their creative potential. Portugal reached the Round of 16 where they lost to eventual champions Spain. What's Happened Since: If Messi's exit from the world stage was a storybook ending, then Cristiano Ronaldo provided one that felt more like a tabloid. Ronaldo, who had already announced that 2026 would be his last World Cup appearance, had a falling out with manager Jorge Jesus and abruptly left the team in September over disagreements about playing. Portugal still won its four Nations League games – including two victories over Erling Haaland's Norway – and looked crisper without Ronaldo up top. Next Opponents: vs. Czechia (Nov. 14); vs. England (Nov. 17) Alexi's Take: "Having Portugal here is a bit of the opposite reasoning for having Argentina where they are at. I guess we could call it the new Portugal, more than likely now without Cristiano Ronaldo. We have seen how good they are, even recently in this window. I feel like a burden, whether they have admitted it or not, is going to be lifted, and they are just going to get better. Nobody's denying all the talent they have, but this incredible weight (or albatross as some people may say) is now gone. I am bullish on them going forward without Cristiano Ronaldo, just maybe not so bullish when it comes to Argentina without Messi." 2026 World Cup Recap: With "Wonderwall" providing the soundtrack, there was belief that it would finally come home. England had its best finish at the men's World Cup since 1990 as it reached the semifinals, losing to ancient rivals Argentina and then to France in the bronze match. Harry Kane scored six times this summer, but Jude Bellingham really came into his own at this tournament, with the round-of-16 win over Mexico at the Estadio Azteca etching his name into Three Lions lore. What's Happened Since: Under manager Thomas Tuchel, there will be expectations as always for a major trophy – whether it's in the Nations League or potentially at the Euros in 2028 as hosts. A loss to Spain in September in a Nations League match shouldn't sour those hopes. Next Opponents: vs. Croatia (Nov. 12); vs. Spain (Nov. 15) Alexi's Take: "It hurts me to say England, but they are just a good team. But they are not at the level of the top two teams. But England is always there, and they are as good – and maybe better – than many other teams, even ones in the past that won the World Cup." FIFA rank: 3 2026 World Cup Recap: The amount of star power in this squad – including forward trio Kylian Mbappé, Ousmane Dembélé, and Michael Olise – had Les Bleus fans thinking this was the team to beat at the tournament. Mbappé scored an astonishing 10 goals at the tournament (making him winner of the Golden Boot for top scorer) and setting a record for most ever in World Cup history with 22. France ran into a brick wall against Spain in the semis but finished in third after a high-scoring consolation match against England. What's Happened Since: With Didier Deschamps stepping down as manager following the World Cup, it felt like an end of an era. But with legend Zinedine Zidane taking over, don't expect France to lose a step – especially with Mbappé, Dembélé, and Olise still in the mix. France won all four of its matches in this window despite Mbappé leaving the team early due to an injury. Next Opponents: vs. Italy (Nov. 12); vs. Türkiye (Nov. 15) Alexi's Take: "This team is just loaded. But the top team did make them look average in the World Cup semifinals." FIFA rank: 12026 World Cup Recap: An improbable run where they only gave up one goal in eight games to win the country's second men's World Cup title ever. Lamine Yamal came into the tournament injured, but La Roja hardly needed the teenage superstar. On their way to the World Cup title, midfield maestro Rodri won the Golden Ball for the tournament's best player and Unai Simón won for the tournament's best keeper. What's Happened Since: Spain's unbeaten streak has now reached 40 games after winning four more times in Nations League action during this past window, including a 3-2 thrilling victory over England at Wembley. Next Opponents: vs. Czechia (Nov. 12); vs. England (Nov. 15)

item.title: Enzo Maresca: 'I Completely Trust' Man City Despite Bombshell Guilty Verdict
item.description: Enzo Maresca has come out in defense of Manchester City’s ownership despite the club being found guilty of breaking the Premier League’s financial rules.
item.content:encoded: Enzo Maresca came out in defense of Manchester City's ownership on Friday, despite the club being found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules in the biggest scandal in the competition's history. The manager Maresca said he had complete trust in City's hierarchy, and dismissed suggestions the club's unprecedented dominance of English soccer had been tainted by the bombshell verdict that it had artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1 billion to help sign some of soccer’s biggest stars. "I completely trust the club in this moment, in the future, always," Maresca said in his first news conference since the findings of an independent panel were published last week. "The reason why I joined this club is because I completely trust 100% the owner, the CEO, the sports director, all the organization, so I don’t have any doubt about that." Maresca was speaking ahead of City's Premier League match with Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. Unsurprisingly the focus was on the verdict, which found the United Arab Emirates-backed team committed almost all of the 115-plus violations it was accused of during a period in which City changed the landscape of the world’s most popular soccer league. City has always denied the charges and has lodged an appeal. "I would like to speak about this situation when we’re going to win the appeal," Maresca said. Asked if the verdict tarnished City's success over more than a decade of dominance, Maresca replied, "Absolutely not." Maresca was hired at the end of last season when former manager Pep Guardiola stepped down after a trophy-laden 10-year tenure. He had previously worked as Guardiola's assistant during the 2023 treble-winning season. Asked if he still would have taken the job had the verdict come out before he became manager, Maresca replied, "100%." "I know the organization from years ago and I know how serious they are. I know that they do the right things," he said. "I trust the club because I trust the people, and this is also the reason why I joined the club. And then there is not another club in the world where I would like to be, so I’m very happy to be here." Maresca's immediate job is to focus the players' minds ahead of the trip to Anfield. "We completely understand the seriousness of the situation. I’m not saying that we don’t understand that. We understand, the players understand. But it’s our duty, our job, to try to control the noise," he said. " "For me and for the players, we can control just the pitch side, the field side. So we are focused on that, and this is what we can do and we can control." Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany, who played for City from 2012-19, has offered guarded support for the club's achievements at the time while also distancing himself from the controversy. Kompany said Friday he was "100% focused" on Bayern and that didn't leave him time "to dwell on other things." "But for me, it’s actually quite simple – I played there for 11 years, and I stand fully behind what we achieved on the field and the feeling we shared as a group of players during that time." he said. "Everything else, I have to be honest, it feels a bit far removed from my reality at the moment." Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: Erling Haaland Wants Manchester City Fans To Be United Amid Guilty Verdict
item.description: Erling Haaland has called on everyone at Manchester City to “stick together" in his first public comments since the club was found guilty of large-scale financial rule-breaking.
item.content:encoded: Erling Haaland called on everyone at Manchester City to "stick together" in his first public comments since the club was found guilty of large-scale financial rule-breaking in the Premier League. City will play Liverpool on Sunday in its first match since the publication of an investigatory panel’s verdict that City artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1 billion from 2009-18 to circumvent financial fair-play rules that restricted rival clubs in that period. City was found guilty by the panel of all 80 of the serious financial charges brought by the Premier League and could be hit with severe sanctions — including being expelled from the top flight. City has lodged an appeal against the findings. In an interview with Sky Sports published Thursday, Haaland — City's most high-profile player — said: "We have to stick together and we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah, stick together, enjoy the ride and smile." Asked what his message would be to City fans traveling to Anfield, where a potentially hostile reception awaits the team, Haaland said: "We have to stick together, we have to stay with each other and we have to stay positive. "No matter what happens in life, we have always have to have a smile. So we have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and then try to enjoy the situation and the game." City manager Enzo Maresca is likely to face more severe questioning Friday when he holds his pre-match news conference with reporters. It will be Maresca's first remarks on the scandal, with domestic soccer having been on hold for the past three weeks because of an extended international break. Premier League Managers Speak On Man City Case The return of the Premier League offers rival team coaches a first opportunity to react to the City case that has rocked the world’s most popular soccer league and is likely to have a major impact on the remainder of the season. They weren't rushing to judgment on Thursday. "We’ve all seen the news. It’s obviously big news," said Frank Lampard, the Coventry manager who played for City for one of the seasons — 2014-15 — that has been under investigation. "Man City are appealing the situation so I guess my reaction is that: what can you say when an appeal is going on? I’m not inside the story, I’m outside it completely — I played for Man City a long time ago, for one year — so we’ll wait and see what the result of the appeal is." Bournemouth manager Marco Rose preferred to stay away from the matter, saying: "I’m a football coach, not a politician," while Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle said he was "not able to judge" as a manager of another club and "there are authorities taking care of it." In a similar vein, Leeds manager Daniel Farke said there were "more qualified people ... able to speak about it." Speaking at the Leaders in Sport conference in London, Leeds chairman Paraag Marathe – president of the club’s U.S.-ownership group, 49ers Enterprises – said he believed "the most just result, I’m sure, will be delivered." "In any sport, you know, everybody wants to play by the same rules," he added, without mentioning City. Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: The Moment Lionel Messi's Homecoming Felt More Than Just A Farewell
item.description: It wasn't a just a tribute nor a simple farewell. It was a homecoming for a hero.
item.content:encoded: ON TUESDAY NIGHT, under the cloudy skies of Buenos Aires, as Argentina sorrowfully said goodbye to Lionel Messi in his final match for the national team, there was a very specific moment that I can’t erase out of my mind. It wasn’t the crowd’s energy chanting his name upon scoring his 126th goal, nor the light drone show that extravagantly produced a tribute for the more than 85,000 witnesses packed into Estadio Más Monumental. It wasn’t Enzo Fernández’s uncontrollable tears or even Messi’s reflective speech where he solemnly remembered his late father as well as his nation. It wasn’t any of this. The moment that truly and fervently grabbed and brought me to tears was when Thiago Messi — Leo’s 13-year-old and oldest son — approached his father during the post-game tributes and embraced him with a hug. Both consoled each other, crying in a sea of emotion because Thiago knew that his father’s impact on the nation had been so powerful that this international retirement was almost too much to take in. But I also think that particular beautiful moment between father and son made Thiago realize the sacrifices his papá had made throughout his career and how after everything Lionel Messi has gone through, it was now time to close the chapter on this incredible story. At 13, Thiago is the same age his father was when he left his home country for Barcelona and I think there was a beautiful sense of understanding from Leo’s eldest son. The hug was a moment of empathy and appreciation as Messi’s successes and triumphs, which include World Cup and Champions League glory and more trophies than any other player in the history of the sport, also came with unmeasurable pain. And that’s why last night was special. Because it wasn’t just about saying, "thank you." It was also about saying, "I understand your sacrifice and I remain grateful for what you gave to the world." LIONEL MESSI'S INTERNATIONAL career cannot be defined simply by goals or assists, nor by the trophies he has accumulated along the way. There simply isn’t a barometer on the planet that can measure his greatness, because what Messi has provided for Argentinians — and the footballing world — is not just about his own excellence. The real beauty is about the obstacles in Messi’s path and how he battled through a series of struggles. From being rejected as an Argentinian after losing a World Cup final and back-to-back Copa América titles between 2014 and 2016 to returning to a road of redemption until winning it all in 2022. Argentina needs to own its role too. During the hardships, to many critics, there was a patriotic rejection against Messi and much of the reason was because Leo was the complete opposite of their original hero, Diego Maradona. The late legend was controversial, loud, funny, charismatic and quintessentially boisterous in a typical Argentinian way, which was everything Messi the introvert wasn’t. Maradona also played in Argentina until he was 21 until he left for Europe. Messi left Rosario as a teenager and for many years, the federation didn’t even know about him. There was, therefore, a deep pain that impacted Leo throughout his career, and it wasn’t until he returned from his first retirement in August 2016, two months after losing the aforementioned Copa América Centenario to Chile, that his nation realized that what Messi needed was love and support. "IF I GOT rid of my demons, I'd lose my angels." Tennessee Williams' saying encapsulates why Messi needed those moments of struggle and rejection in order for us to fully appreciate the light of his greatness. And that’s why Tuesday night in Buenos Aires, in front of 85,000 people and millions more watching from around the world, the tribute was not a farewell. It was a homecoming. So what happens next? What do we make of this empty void? How do we react to the future of not just Argentinian football on the international stage, but of the entire global game? How do we appreciate art without its painter? I think the answer is already here. From Lamine Yamal’s brilliance and Erling Haaland’s preponderance to Michael Olise’s dazzle and Jude Bellingham’s genius, the world’s game is in good hands. World-class talent, as I have alluded to, will come and go and we will see beautiful moments from many players for the next few decades. And if we feel like reliving it, we can always take a trip to Miami — at least in the near future. But know this and remember it well. There will never exist another player like Lionel Messi because what he gave us wasn’t just about his own brilliant self. It was also about ourselves and how, for 90 minutes, a diminutive, introverted Argentinian from Rosario made us feel like giants.

item.title: USA's Next Generation Lived Up To The Hype; Now The Real Work Begins
item.description: Mauricio Pochettino had a plan for the U.S. men's national team entering this international window, and it could hardly have gone much better.
item.content:encoded: ALLIANZ FIELD (St. Paul, Minn.) — Mauricio Pochettino had a plan. Ahead of FIFA’s first international window of the 2030 World Cup cycle, the coach of the U.S. men’s national team knew that the Americans’ four exhibition games in late September and early October presented a unique opportunity to take a long look at the next generation of American talent before games that matter resume in November with the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals. He summoned the kids. He played them all, with 20-year-old Cole Campbell, who became the 13 and final previously uncapped invitee to debut for the USA when he entered as a substitute in the second half of Tuesday’s 1-0 win over Canada in the Twin Cities. Pochettino got goals from teenagers in all four matches. Mathis Albert became the youngest scorer in program history, then saw his record smashed just four days later by fellow 17-year-old Cavan Sullivan. Justin Ellis, 19, scored the winner Tuesday against the Reds, his second goal in as many starts, having also found the net in the 4-1 win over Peru on Sept. 26 that started the USA on its way to a clean four-game sweep. Julian Hall, 18, scored in his first three international appearances, including game-winners over Chile and Peru. The plan could hardly have gone much better. "The players, I think they deserve the credit," Pochettino said after Tuesday’s contest. "I’m not talking only about the results. I’m talking about the way that we competed. "I think it was amazing," the Argentine continued, "to play always with the same intensity, with the same commitment, with the same passion. That is something that we need to keep." Surely he needs to keep some of the kids around, too. With the U.S. youth national teams idle this window, Pochettino didn’t have to consider the needs of the U.S. under-23 squad. That will change in November, when Olympic coach Steve Cherundolo convenes a group of players that will compete for the majority of roster spots at the 2028 Summer Games in Los Angeles — an event the U.S. Soccer Federation is desperate to have a strong showing in on home soil. So Pochettino’s strategy was always to give big minutes to youngsters like Hall and Ellis with the senior team early this autumn. The former Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea boss revealed after Tuesday’s victory that that would’ve been the case even if World Cup striker Ricardo Pepi hadn’t gotten hurt playing for Dutch champs PSV Eindhoven a day before he was scheduled to arrive at the USSF’s training base outside of Atlanta. In November, the original idea went, most of the youngsters would return to the U-23s or even the U.S. U-20s, which in August qualified for next year’s FIFA U-20 World Cup in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. Their performances this month could alter that thinking, however. Following the 3-0 win over Mexico, Pochettino told me that it "was a fantastic problem" to have. "Having a plan, you can adjust things and fix situations or change if you are seeing that you need to change," he said on Tuesday. Still, Pochettino won’t have the luxury of not caring about results next month. The Americans learned earlier Tuesday that they will face 2026 World Cup participants Haiti over two legs in mid-November, with a spot in next March’s Nations League finals on the line. "They made the World Cup for a reason: because they're a tough team," U.S. defender Chris Richards, who started the 2-1 win over Haiti in last year’s Concacaf Gold Cup, said of Les Grenadiers. "Got to go in there with the same mindset we've had throughout this camp, and we have to earn a victory to get to March." "We're very excited for it," the Premier Leaguer added. "It's another chance to prove ourselves. And whoever will be at that camp, I know we'll go in there with our heads held high after what we did in this camp, and hopefully, gonna get two wins." One camp into the new cycle, the competition for places should be fierce — especially if 2026 cycle mainstays such as Pepi, Folarin Balogun, Weston McKennie and Christian Pulisic are all healthy and available and performing well for their European clubs. "Obviously, there are a lot of new faces, and they all had great energy and worked very hard while they were here," two-time World Cup veteran Gio Reyna said. "It definitely brings competition, which is what we all need. And I think it's great for the upcoming cycle to push everybody."

item.title: Messi's Final Match For Argentina Sees The GOAT Score One Last Time
item.description: Lionel Messi turns his official farewell match for Argentina into a gala performance, scoring one last time.
item.content:encoded: Lionel Messi turned his official farewell to Argentina into a gala performance, contributing a penalty and two assists in a 3-0 win over Benin in an international friendly on Tuesday at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, where the crowd offered a deafening final ovation to the genius who, for over two decades, defined the footballing pulse of a nation. In front of 85,000 fans, the superstar capped off an international career spanning 21 years, 126 goals, a 2022 World Cup victory, and two Copa América titles. Orchestrating The Win Following a corner kick taken Messi, defender Nicolas Otamendi connected with a header to open the scoring in the 48th minute. Messi then provided an assist to young talent Nicolas Paz, who paid tribute to the star with an exquisite left-foot finish in the 61st. Ten minutes later, Messi buried a left-foot penalty into the top corner, adding to his tally as the Albiceleste’s all-time leading scorer. "Olé, olé, Messi," the crowd chanted in his honor. Passing The Torch Despite still playing at a high level at age 39, Messi announced on Aug. 31 that the end of his time with Argentina was set. Messi played his final match — his 208th for Argentina — amid a spectacular fireworks display. He wore a special edition Albiceleste jersey featuring wider vertical stripes than the standard design, a giant sun, and a golden No. 10 on the back. The back detail featured a goat’s horns in the print — a nod to the "GOAT," referencing both the animal and his status as the "Greatest of All Time." Ten minutes after kickoff, the referee paused the match to honor the Argentine captain. Rivals and teammates approached to greet him while fans rose for a standing ovation. Messi raised his hand in acknowledgment. "Come, come, sing with me, and a friend you’ll find; hand in hand with Leo Messi, we’ll all celebrate the victory," the crowd sang to him. From Heartbreak To World Cup Glory A successor to the legendary Diego Maradona, Messi made his debut for the senior national team in 2005. But his journey was fraught with frustration until 2022, when he finally lifted the World Cup — a triumph that secured his place in the pantheon of the sport’s greatest players and cemented his status as a national hero in Argentina. Accompanied by his sons Thiago, Mateo, and Ciro, Messi was overcome with emotion as the Argentine national anthem played, sung by a veteran of the 1982 Falklands War. Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez tried to comfort him by placing an arm around his shoulders. Devoted Fans And Moving Tributes "It’s not a goodbye, it’s a ‘farewell forever,’ Captain" — that was the message Rebeca Arias and Daniel Lema emblazoned on a hat designed for the occasion. On the brim, they drew various depictions of Messi corresponding to each of the six World Cups he contested. The young couple traveled more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from their native Tucumán to witness his final performance. "We believe this is a unique moment. It’s all worth it — being here, making the journey we did. Something like this might never happen again with a player," Arias remarked. In the last World Cup, Messi went close to another title, falling just short after a 1-0 defeat to Spain in the final. However, the runner-up finish didn't overshadow his remarkable performance in the tournament — featuring eight goals and four assists. His contribution was so pivotal that Messi has once again entered the conversation for the Ballon d’Or, competing against the two top contenders to succeed him: Spaniard Lamine Yamal and Frenchman Kylian Mbappé. The Argentine star remains the only footballer to have won the award eight times. Messi Receives Honorary Doctorate Before his farewell at the stadium, Messi received an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires (UBA), a public institution. The academic institution presented the honor at the national team’s training complex in the suburb of Ezeiza. The star was awarded a diploma and a medal in recognition of his performance with the national team, as well as his influence both on and off the pitch. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: It's A Clean Sweep: 4 Takeaways From USA's Victory Over Canada
item.description: USA 1-0 Canada: 4 Takeaways
item.content:encoded: ALLIANZ FIELD (St. Paul, Minn.) — A fourth win and as many games for the U.S. men’s national team to kick off the 2030 FIFA World Cup cycle. The Stars and Stripes beat rivals Canada, 1-0, on Tuesday in the Twin Cities on a first-half goal by 19-year-old striker Justin Ellis — a win that comes on the heels of convincing victories over the last 12 days against Peru, Chile and historic nemesis Mexico. Here are my takeaways, plus post-game reaction from the players, USA coach Mauricio Pochettino and Canada's American boss Jesse Marsch. 1. The Teenagers Are A Force Back on Sept. 26 in Orlando, the 19-year-old Ellis scored the USA’s first goal less than four minutes into what turned into a 4-1 rout of Peru. Julian Hall (18) and Mathis Albert (17) scored three days later in St. Louis in a 4-2 victory over Chile. Hall hit the target again in Saturday’s 3-0 win over Mexico; in the second half of the same match in Glendale, Arizona, 17-year-old Cavan Sullivan broke Albert’s four-day old record to become the youngest scorer in more than a century of U.S. men’s soccer. That theme continued on Tuesday. Ellis earned his second start of this four-match set, and, despite being hobbled by a challenge by acting Canadian captain Stephen Eustáquio midway through the first half, limped back onto the field and promptly got on the end of a cross by Alex Freeman, his former teammate with Orlando City SC. It was the hosts only shot during a foul-laden first 45 minutes. Pochettino replaced Ellis with Hall for the start of the second half; Ellis left the stadium to have what a team spokesperson called a right lower leg contusion. He wasn’t the only teenager to start the game, though, as Albert, who entered as a sub in each of the Americans' first three outings this camp, made his first appearance in the coach’s 11. And towering 6-foot-7 center back Neil Pierre, 18, came in to help preserve the clean sheet. "They need to be ready to take the opportunity," Pochettino said of the youngsters in general before mentioning the two strikers in paricular. "To assess and to see Julian and Justin was always the plan for us." 2. U.S. Snaps Winless Streak Against Its Northern Neighbors Three days after halting a two-match losing streak against El Tri, the Stars and Stripes broke another run of futility against another cross-border rival. "I give credit to the way the U.S. defended," said Marsch, a former USA midfielder and assistant coach. "They bent, but they didn't break." Besides a shootout win in the 2023 Gold Cup quarterfinals — a result that FIFA officially considers a tie — the U.S. had gone six tries without besting Canada and lost the last two meetings between the sides before Tuesday. So this triumph was a welcome one for U.S. fans and a potentially important psychological one for the American players — especially given the makeup of Pochettino’s relatively inexperienced September/October roster. That could be important if these sides meet again next year in either the Concacaf Nations League in March or the Gold Cup next summer. Or both. 3. What’s Next For The Kids? With the competitive games of this World Cup cycle beginning next month (more on that below), it will be fascinating to see which of the youngsters stick with the senior team and which ones return to either the U.S. under-20 or -23 national teams, the latter of which will double as the 2028 U.S. Olympic squad when the Los Angeles games kick off two summers from now. The assumption is that many of those on Pochettino’s roster for the 2026 World Cup who were either injured, returning from injury, settling in with new clubs or are known quantities come back into the fold. That long list includes Folarin Balogun, Weston McKennie, Ricardo Pepi, Christian Pulisic and Tim Weah — players who have long been mainstays for the Americans, in some cases for multiple World Cups. Still, some will probably stay with the varsity. Hall is probably the likeliest candidate, though he’s not alone. It’s not just the teenagers, either. Diego Kochen’s performance in goal vs. Mexico could win him another look. Same for older players like keeper Brian Schwake, who made four saves on the way to posting a clean sheet Tuesday in his first start, and fellow 25-year-old George Campbell, who started his second match of the window and third overall. "They seemed pretty comfortable from the beginning" of camp, veteran defender Chris Richards said of the new guard. "It's been it's been a lot of fun getting to know everybody — and not just on the field, but off the field." 4. Haiti Looms In Next Month’s Nations League Quarterfinals The U.S. won the first three editions of the semi-annual Concacaf competition, hoisting the trophy in 2021, 2023 and 2024. It strolled past Jamaica over two legs to return to the final four just a month after Pochettino took over the program, winning a competitive game in Kingston for just the second time ever. An upset by Panama ended the trophy streak in the semis in March of last year, and this same Canada squad added insult to injury by beating the Americans in the third place match at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles. Pochettino & Co. would like to put that right in the same venue next March, when the Nations League finals return to Southern California. But they’ll need to get past a World Cup participant to get there, as Haiti was confirmed earlier Tuesday as the USA’s opponent in next month’s quarterfinals. Even with Haiti’s home leg of the two-match, total-goals-wins series to be played in a neutral country because of severe security concerns in the Caribbean nations, beating Les Grenadiers isn’t a forgone conclusion. Although the U.S. hasn’t lost to the Haitians since 1973, their five most recent meetings have either ended even or with a one-goal American win. The Americans could learn where the opening match will be held as soon as Wednesday. The back end of the home-and-home is scheduled for Nov. 17 in Cincinnati. "It's going to be a tough opponent," said U.S. captain Tyler Adams, who was a member of the U.S. team that defeated the Haitians 2-1 in the group stage of last year's Gold Cup. "That was a really, really tough game, one of those typical scrappy Concacaf games. So we need to be up for it."

item.title: As Lionel Messi's Argentina Career Ends, How It Started Is Worth Remembering
item.description: There will never be another player like him. I hope you enjoyed his greatness and reliving his legacy.
item.content:encoded: The first time I ever watched Lionel Messi play soccer couldn’t have been more anticlimactic. Though the player now generally accepted as the greatest in the history of the planet’s most popular sport had already made his first team debut for Barcelona by this time, the setting was far from the bright lights at the then 90,000-seat Camp Nou, Europe’s largest stadium. Messi was 18, the second-youngest member of Argentina’s under-20 national team, when he and his teammates met the United States on June 11, 2005, in both countries' first match of what was then called the FIFA World Youth Championship. Arke Stadion in the small Dutch city of Enschede was barely a third full. The kid who’d become the GOAT was on the bench when Chad Barrett — who’d go on to win one senior cap for the Americans — scored the eventual winner late in six minutes before halftime. Messi, still mostly unknown except to soccer dorks like me, didn’t do much when he entered in the second half of the game, which I watched on a 13-inch television in my cubicle at ESPN The Magazine’s midtown Manhattan office. Of course, Messi started the rest of the way, finishing as the tournament’s top scorer and MVP as Argentina claimed the title. A year later, I saw Messi live for the first time; he scored for Barça in a 4-1 friendly win over the New York Red Bulls. As he shyly answered questions in Spanish post-game, floppy brown hair hanging over his eyes, I was struck by how tiny he was. This is the guy who some Argentines were already calling Diego Maradona’s heir apparent? "He’s the closest one yet," Bob Bradley told me when I asked about the comparison a year after that. Bradley, who had just been named coach of the U.S. men’s national team, is as serious as they come. But he couldn't help light up at the mere mention of Messi, who his squad would face in the opening match of the 2007 Copa América in Venezuela. I used the quote in a short blurb about Messi, writing that the youngster was well on his way to eventually eclipsing Barcelona teammate Ronaldinho as the best player in the world. Over the almost two decades since, he’s vastly exceeded that prediction and most others, too. MESSI'S LEGACY WAS cemented during the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, but it's easy to forget now what the mood was like inside Lusail Stadium with less than 30 minutes remaining against Mexico in the Albiceleste’s second group stage match that November outside of Doha. Billed as Messi’s last chance to win the ultimate prize in sports — he’d said he’d retire after the tourney, win or lose — Argentina was in danger of being eliminated with one first round match to go. Then Messi popped up out of nowhere and stroked the ball past El Tri keeper Guillermo Ochoa, his first of eight goals — including two in the final win over France — on the way to his country’s only World Cup title since Maradona’s in 1986. With that golden trophy in hand, Messi promptly changed his mind about hanging up his boots. I was at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami in 2024 when he hoisted the Copa América for the second time in three years. In July, I watched him break down in tears on the field as Spain beat Argentina in extra time to wrest the World Cup away from the 39-year-old. La Roja were worthy champs, yet a wave of sadness engulfed me as I realized that this was probably the last time anyone would ever see Messi wearing that famous baby-blue and white striped No. 10 shirt. Messi was still his side’s best player that day. Now, with Messi having played his send-off match with Argentina (and scoring one last goal from the penalty spot), I’m filled with gratitude for having been able to cover his career almost from start to finish. Most soccer lovers have never watched him play in person. I don’t take for granted that I’ve seen him so many times I’ve lost count. l've been there for the downs — the shootout loss to the Netherlands in São Paulo in the semifinals of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, another to Chile in the Copa final in New Jersey in 2016, after which an emotional Messi vowed never to play for his country again before changing his mind for the first time — as well as the once seemingly unreadable heights of 2022 and ’24. It’s still surreal to see Messi in MLS and probably will be until he walks away for good, hopefully not before his current contract with Inter Miami expires in 2028. Watching Lionel Messi play soccer — whether it's on a screen or in the stands or a press box — is a privilege that never gets old. There will never be another player like him. Enjoy it as long as you can.

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Is Not Retiring, Blames Coach Jorge Jesus For Portugal Walkout
item.description: Cristiano Ronaldo is not following Lionel Messi into international retirement just yet.
item.content:encoded: Cristiano Ronaldo is not following Lionel Messi into international retirement just yet. The Portugal superstar said he will remain available to play for his national team, despite having walked out on the squad during the current international window. In a long statement issued through the Portuguese media Tuesday, Ronaldo said recently hired coach Jorge Jesus had not been true to his word about when he would play the striker in the latest round of Nations League matches. Still, the 41-year-old Ronaldo said he owed his teammates an apology and expects to receive a punishment. "I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," Ronaldo said. He added: "Therefore, if I am physically fit, playing for my club, hopefully scoring goals, then after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team." Ronaldo said he had agreed to a plan for managing his playing time and that he expected the coach to publicly clarify the situation and accept responsibility. He said Jesus did not follow through and instead spoke aggressively at a press conference, causing a breakdown of trust. Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: Lionel Messi's Farewell To Argentina: A Look At The GOAT's Historic World Cup Career
item.description: As Lionel Messi says farewell to the Argentina, let's look back at his legendary World Cup career.
item.content:encoded: The time has come for Lionel Messi to don his Argentina jersey for one last time. The greatest of all time announced on Aug. 31 that he would retire from international play, culminating a 22-year career with Argentina that included a World Cup title. Across six World Cup appearances, Messi has led Argentina to the quarterfinals or better five times and reached the final three times. His résumé includes six World Cup appearances, 34 matches, 21 goals, 12 assists, and countless records, many of which he extended during his historic tournament this summer. His legacy on the tournament’s biggest stage is unlike anything the sport has ever seen. Argentina will face Benin in an international friendly in Buenos Aires at 7 p.m. ET. In honor of Messi's final match with Argentina, let’s look back at his remarkable World Cup journey, starting with his all-time tournament records, then revisiting each of his six appearances on soccer's biggest stage.
