item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Reportedly Won't Play For Portugal Under New Coach Jorge Jesus
item.description: Cristiano Ronaldo has threatened to not represent Portugal under new coach Jorge Jesus.
item.content:encoded: Portugal wants Cristiano Ronaldo to know he's welcome back to the national team, if he so desires. The issue? It's not something he desires — not so long as Jorge Jesus is the coach. According to a report from ESPN on Tuesday, the 41-year-old superstar has issued the Portuguese Football Federation an ultimatum, threatening not to return to the national team under Jesus. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus and federation president Pedro Proença have downplayed the "misunderstanding" that led to Ronaldo’s decision to leave the national team's training camp last week, saying after a 2-1 win over Norway in the Nations League on Sunday that the veteran star can return whenever he wants. "We are talking about the greatest player of all time, a player who has given more than two decades to Portuguese soccer," Proença told Portuguese television channel RTP. "He will always be part of this squad if he is technically fit to play. Cristiano knows this. He knows that is the sentiment. What happened was a misunderstanding that needs to be resolved internally." Ronaldo walked out on Portugal’s training camp on Wednesday, hours after Jesus said the veteran star would not start in a game against Denmark in the Nations League. Jesus had kept Ronaldo on the bench in a previous match despite saying he would play. Ronaldo said after leaving that in due course he would "tell the Portuguese people the truth about the reasons" behind his departure, but has not commented on the situation since. Jesus said Sunday he had no reason to apologize to anyone, and that he would call up Ronaldo again for the next international break if the player wants to come back. "I don’t know what Cris will decide," Jesus said after Portugal’s win. "To me, there was never an issue. There are non-negotiable principles for a coach, but since there were no issues regarding my authority, for me, if Cris wants to return, he will be eligible for the next call-up, as long as he is playing for Al Nassr. It's up to him." Proença said there will be time for everyone to sit down and discuss the situation. "Ronaldo is a symbol of our country. He is a Portuguese icon, an absolutely extraordinary player who could have ended his international career after the World Cup but chose not to out of love for the national team," Proença said. While Ronaldo has said that the 2026 World Cup was his final one, he has not spoken on his future in international play. Jesus, who was hired in July following Portugal's exit at the World Cup, said at the time of his hiring that he needed to discuss Ronaldo's future with him at some point. "That’s a conversation we’re both going to have. What does he want to do for the future of his career?" The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Balogun: Premier League 'Definitely' Still An Option After Collapsed Everton Move
item.description: United States striker Folarin Balogun hasn't given up on a return to the Premier League, a month after his deadline-day move to Everton fell apart.
item.content:encoded: United States men's national team striker Folarin Balogun hasn't given up on a return to the Premier League, a month after his deadline-day move to Everton fell apart. Asked by talkSPORT whether a Premier League move still interested him, the 25-year-old called it a possibility. "I was close to a transfer," Balogun said. "It didn't materialise, but for sure it's definitely an option." Balogun, who came through Arsenal's academy before joining Monaco on a permanent transfer in 2023, remains with the Ligue 1 club after a summer that put him at the center of two major controversies. "Football has many twists and turns as we've seen after the World Cup," Balogun said. What Happened With Balogun's Everton Move? Everton had a deal in place to sign Balogun from Monaco for a reported £40 million ($54 million), but it collapsed in the final minutes of the Sept. 1 transfer deadline. Monaco sporting director Thiago Scuro later laid out the timeline at a news conference. According to Scuro, Balogun took his medical at Everton that afternoon, and about three hours later, Everton came back with questions about the results that he said "made no sense at all" to Monaco's medical staff and the player's own doctors. After the two clubs' medical teams talked, Everton said it was ready to complete the signing. At the last moment, Balogun decided not to sign. Scuro said the striker told Monaco he wasn't comfortable committing to a long contract after Everton raised doubts about his health. Balogun's World Cup Red Card Controversy Balogun was the United States' top scorer at the World Cup with three goals, but his tournament ended in controversy. He was sent off in the Americans' 2-0 round-of-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina, which normally carries an automatic one-game suspension, but FIFA suspended the ban for one year, clearing Balogun to face Belgium in the round of 16. FIFA's disciplinary committee cited a rule that allows it to suspend sanctions. Balogun played against Belgium, but the U.S. lost 4-1 in Seattle, ending its run on home soil. He later acknowledged that the outside noise around FIFA's decision had affected the team mentally, the AP reported. How Has Balogun Started The Season At Monaco? Monaco has thrived without him. The club won four of its first five Ligue 1 matches and drew the other to go top of the table, sitting five points clear of defending champion Paris Saint-Germain after beating PSG 2-1 in Paris on Sept. 4. Balogun made his first appearance since the World Cup as a late substitute in a 2-1 home win over Lens on Sept. 18. Paris Brunner, a 20-year-old striker, has filled the void with six goals this season. Scuro said after the Everton collapse that Monaco was still open to selling Balogun to clubs in markets where transfer windows remained open, per the AP. Saudi Arabia's window stays open until Oct. 12, but for now Balogun remains at Monaco, where he has two years left on his contract. Monaco hosts Toulouse on Saturday, Oct. 10.

item.title: Tired USA Meets Canada Aiming To Kick Off 2030 World Cup Cycle With 4th Straight win
item.description: After trouncing Mexico on Satuday, the U.S. men's soccer team finishes this four-game FIFA window against another North American rival in Canada.
item.content:encoded: As palpable as the euphoria was among the Americans players who sauntered down the tunnel beneath State Farm Stadium following the USA’s 3-0 dismantling of Mexico last Saturday night in Arizona, so was the exhaustion. There was no hooting or hollering. The smiles were tired ones. Before walking into the desert night, playmaker Gio was asked how he’d celebrate the Stars and Stripes most lopsided win against its arch nemesis since his father Claudio’s goal capped a 4-0 victory in 1995. The 23-year-old didn’t hesitate. "I'm gonna go to sleep," Reyna deadpanned. Mauricio Pochettino’s young U.S. team can’t rest quite yet. Led by a fresh generation of young players — including teenagers Cavan Sullivan and Julian Hall, who both scored against Mexico — the Americans are 3-0 so far during this extended, 16-day-long FIFA international window. They’ve managed 11 goals over those exhibitions, including multigoal strolls over South American foes Peru and Chile. But before Pochettino’s players pack up this camp and return to their clubs, the American men’s other big rival, Canada, looms on Tuesday night in Minnesota. (Kickoff at 8 p.m. ET.) Once a regional also-ran, the U.S. hasn’t beaten its northern neighbors in six tries dating to 2021; the USA’s shootout victory in the 2023 Gold Cup quarterfinals counts officially as a tie. They’ve lost two straight to Canada heading into Tuesday’s contest at Allianz Field in St. Paul, including last year under Pochettino in the Concacaf Nations League Finals’ consolation game. So much has happened since then. The United States and Canada co-hosted the World Cup over the summer along with Mexico, with all three North American squads reaching the round of 16. Both teams are different even since then; Pochettino’s current roster is almost four years younger than the one he named for soccer’s marquee quadrennial tournament. "It’s a new chapter," the Argentine said on the eve of the match. Naturally, Pochettino and his players want to beat the Canadians, break the Americans' five-year winless streak and complete the four-game sweep. But it’s not the coaching staff’s only priority. The Reds have played just two times so far this window and have done far less travel. They’re better rested. Pochettino must plan accordingly. "After three games, [the players are] not in the best condition," Pochettino said. "But we cannot change the reality. We need to adapt to the reality and be ready to compete. "The result," he continued, "Is important. But it's not our principal objective." Stylistically, Canada will provide a different challenge for the U.S. than any of the first three September/October tests. Led by American and former U.S. player and assistant coach Jesse Marsch, the Reds are supremely athletic. They press with abandon, are deadly on the counterattack and take advantage of their scoring chances. "I know Jesse very well, I respect him, and I like him like a coach," Pochettino said Monday. "It’s always difficult to play against teams that he coaches. It's very intense…yes, it's a very good challenge for us." He also called Canadian goal machine Jonathan David, "one of the greatest strikers today in the world." "When we were at different clubs, he was always on our radar to try to sign him," the former Chelsea, Paris Saint-Germain and Tottenham manager said. "Now seeing him in La Liga, in a club like Atlético Madrid with a coach like Diego Simeone, is fantastic." Meantime, the U.S. has been paced by Hall, who has three goals in his first three international games. World Cup strikers. The 18-year-old has stood in for World Cup strikers Folarin Balogun, Ricardo Pepi and Haji Wright, who are either hurt or returning from injury. Mixing inexperienced youngsters — 20-year-old Cole Campbell, who’s been nursing a minor ailment, is the only one of the 28 players invited to this camp who hasn’t yet seen the field — alongside veterans like Chris Richards and captain Tyler Adams has been the theme for the U.S. as it starts down the long and winding path toward the 2030 FIFA World Cup. It will be the same on Tuesday, no matter the opponent. " I think we all know what it means to play against Mexico and Canada," Pochettino said. "We need to be focused in our performance. It's not, ‘Oh, we need to win.’ We need to win. Yes, of course. "But the journey is the most important" thing, he added. "That is our focus now."

item.title: One Last Dance? Messi Set for Emotional Argentina Farewell in Buenos Aires
item.description: Argentina fans are confident there is a bright future beyond Lionel Messi as the team's most influential player of the last two decades prepares to bid farewell.
item.content:encoded: Argentina fans are confident there is a bright future beyond Lionel Messi as the team's most influential player of the last two decades prepares to bid farewell. The 39-year-old superstar will play his final match for Argentina on Tuesday — a friendly against Benin at Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires — marking a pivotal moment in the country's football. Messi leaves behind an extraordinary legacy, including the 2022 World Cup title, two more World Cup finals (2014, 2026), two Copa América trophies (2021, 2024), an Olympic gold medal (2008), and 125 goals as the national team’s all-time leading scorer. His international retirement raises an inevitable question: Can Argentina remain among the global elite, or is a long trophy drought — reminiscent of the 35-year dry spell following Diego Maradona’s departure — on the horizon? "Messi leaves behind something unequaled," national coach Lionel Scaloni says. "We have to keep playing, but the feeling of having him on the pitch is unique. I’ve never seen anyone else convey what he does on a football field, and that is what we’re going to miss." However, Scaloni — who is in advanced negotiations to renew his contract for another four years — looks beyond Messi with optimism: "The Argentine national team will endure. We will remain at a high level, I have no doubt about that." In the first two post-World Cup matches without Messi, Argentina dazzled in the past week with resounding victories against Bolivia 4-0 and Burkina Faso 7-0. Despite the opponents’ stature, the matches offered compelling glimpses of what lies ahead. Alongside established stars like Emiliano Martinez, Cristian Romero, Enzo Fernandez, and Lautaro Martinez, an exciting wave of new talent emerged — creative midfielders Nicolas Paz and Franco Mastantuono, and wingers Gianluca Prestianni and Leonel Flores. Flores is a Boca Juniors youth player who made his professional debut just two months ago and has already earned senior national team experience. "There’s a changing of the guard; maybe we have to play differently now, not thinking in terms of ‘Messi and 10 others,’ but rather as a unified team," supporter Cristian Versalles, 55, told the AP after watching the victory over Burkina Faso on Saturday. His son, Ramiro, 23, added, "Given the number of players coming through, there’s definitely a new generation ready to step up. Nico Paz is the heir apparent." Paz, playing out of Italian club Como, was one of the scorers. Also at the friendly and wearing the No. 19 jersey — the same one Messi wore during his senior national team debut in 2005 — 10-year-old fan Uzzi Rivero admitted, "It makes me really sad that he doesn’t play for Argentina anymore." However, the youngster scowled at the suggestion that Argentina might face a trophy-less era following Messi's retirement. Another fan, Valentina Gago, 20, said: "I'm excited about Argentina without Messi; my favorite player is Lautaro Martínez. It’s not the same as Messi but I love him just the same." With his goal against Burkina Faso, Inter Milan captain Lautaro Martínez ranks as Argentina’s third-highest all-time goal-scorer with 42. "As long as the players are eager to give their all for the shirt, for me, Argentina will remain a contender," Gago said. The world will find out at the 2028 Copa América. Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: Cavan Sullivan, USMNT's Youngest Goalscorer, Is Just Getting Started
item.description: Mature beyond his years on the field, Cavan Sullivan looks and sounds like just about any other 17-year-old off it.
item.content:encoded: STATE FARM STADIUM (Glendale, Ariz.) — With his USA jersey slung over his shoulder and the history-making ball in hand, Cavan Sullivan almost looked overwhelmed as he fielded questions from a throng of reporters in the bowels of the 60,00 seat arena he had just about silenced an hour before with one swing of his right foot. During his 65 minutes on the field in Saturday’s 3-0 drubbing of Mexico, he was anything but. Sullivan, who had only turned 17 just five days earlier, became the youngest goalscorer in the century-plus history of the U.S. men’s national team, helping the Americans secure their largest margin of victory over their biggest rival in more than 30 years despite an overwhelmingly pro-El Tri crowd in greater Phoenix. "That wasn't the way I pictured scoring a goal," said Sullivan, whose defensive pressure forced Mexico keeper Jose Rangel into an errant pass that the youngster intercepted and then coolly lofted over Rangel's head and into the net before being mobbed by the entire U.S. bench. "But the celebration was." Though Sullivan has only officially been a senior national team player for a week, it’s clear that he belongs at this level. In his Sept. 26 debut against Peru and last Tuesday vs. Chile, he showed glimpses of the attacking ability that has made the Philadelphia Union academy graduate one of the most productive players in MLS since the domestic league returned from its World Cup break in mid-July. "I think we just got to stop talking about his age," U.S. captain Tyler Adams said. "He's here for a reason." It’s the reason Manchester City struck a deal with the Union for Sullivan to move to the English titans next year — depending, of course, on the outcome of its appeal of financial cheating charges leveled by the Premier League. Yet coach Mauricio Pochettino has been just as impressed by Sullivan’s attitude, work ethic and his commitment to precisely the sort of defensive work that directly led to Saturday's record-breaking strike. "He's a fighter. He's a warrior," Pochettino said. "It’s difficult to find this type of player with a tremendous [offensive] quality, with the ball in possession, and then [the willingness to be] chasing people and recovering the ball. "That is what my impression is after nearly three weeks together," the former Chelsea, Tottenham and Paris Saint-Germain manager added. "It’s unbelievable to have a player like this. I think it's fantastic news for the USA. I hope that he continues growing in that way." "The thing I always was told by my dad growing up was to try and make offense out of defense," Sullivan said. "Obviously, I'm an offensive player, but you're always in the best spots when you win the ball during the press. It's taken time to get better at my defensive work, and I still have a lot to do and a lot to improve on. But yeah, it's a great moment." And not just for Sullivan. The other two Philadelphia players on this young U.S. roster were among the first reserves to reach their teammate after he pumped his fists and ran to the corner flag and slid on his knees before disappearing into a pile of bodies. "To see him so excited, celebrating, coming to us," 18-year-old central defender Neil Pierre said. "He was dreaming of that forever." "Just happy for Cavan, happy that he got his first goal for the national team," added fullback Frankie Westfield. "But I know there's more to come for him, and I'm looking forward to seeing what else he can do." Sullivan didn’t know exactly what to do after the match. Mature beyond his years on the field, he looks and sounds like just about any other 17-year-old off it. After the final whistle sounded, he searched the crowd for his parents and older brother Quinn, who also plays for the Union and who won three senior caps for the U.S. squad last year before a serious knee injury cut short his season. Before the younger Sullivan was whisked away to the team bus and some much-needed sleep before the U.S. heads to Minnesota to take on Canada on Tuesday in this final game of this new, extended four-match FIFA window, he was asked a final question. What will he do with that ball? "Just sort of, I guess, get it signed by the guys," he said, almost sheepishly. "I don't really know what to do with it, to be honest."

item.title: History Made By Cavan Sullivan: 4 Takeaways From USA's Win Over Mexico
item.description: A statement win over your biggest rival? The USA's youngsters shined against Mexico.
item.content:encoded: STATE FARM STADIUM (Glendale, Ariz.) — The U.S. men’s soccer team trounced Mexico, its fiercest rival and FIFA's No. 10 ranked nation, 3-0 in Saturday’s exhibition match here in front of a heavily pro El Tri crowd of more than 60,000 at the home of the NFL’s Arizona Cardinals. Eighteen-year-old forward Julian Hall scored for the third straight game, 17-year-old Cavan Sullivan added the second and Malik Tillman rounded out the scoring with just a few minutes remaining. Here are my takeaways, plus post-game reaction from U.S. coach Mauricio Pochettino and his players. Last weekend against Peru, Cavan Sullivan became the second-youngest player to start in U.S. men's national team history. On Saturday, he notched an even more impressive milestone when he pounced on an errant pass by Jose Rangel and chipped the Mexico keeper to give the Americans a dos-a-cero lead — the youngest goalscorer in the 113-year history of the program. "He's a talented player with enormous quality, but with a very good balance in possession and out of possession," Pochettino said. "He's a fighter. He's a warrior. It's difficult to find this type of player. "Happy for him, happy for the team," the coach added. "I like what he said [on TNT's broadcast] after the game, that the most important thing was the result. He's learning every day. That is a good thing." Until losing back-to-back games to Mexico in 2024 and ’25, the U.S. had dominated its southern neighbor this decade, beating El Tri in three straight Concacaf Nations League Finals and the Gold Cup final in 2021. The pendulum swung back after Pochettino took over as coach, though that was hardly his fault, with an understrength U.S. squad falling in a so-called friendly in Guadalajara and in the 2025 Gold Cup final in Houston. After beating the Peruvians and Chile decisively late last month, Pochettino cautioned on Friday that there would be downs as well as ups for this unusually young roster, the first one of the 2030 World Cup cycle. But the kids didn’t get the memo, growing into the match against Mexico and taking the scoring chances they were presented with. That’s a hugely encouraging sign going forward. "Mexico is a great team," Pochettino said. "They forced us to play backwards. We never connected, we were losing all the duels. And then we started to grow after 15-20 minutes." "We had to adapt in different ways," U.S. captain Tyler Adams said. "At halftime we kind of regrouped…I thought it was a complete team performance in a lot of different facets of the game. We had some challenges to defend. I think we defended all right for most of the part, and then obviously scored some good goals." It’s possible that the 18-year-old Red Bull New York striker wouldn’t even have been on Pochettino’s roster for Saturday’s contest. World Cup starter Folarin Balogun and one of his backups, Haji Wright, were not called in this window. Hall might not have played nearly as much if Ricardo Pepi, who appeared in all five games during the Americans’ run to the round of 16, hadn’t gotten hurt after Pochettino named his roster back on Sept. 17. No matter. Hall has taken every opportunity he’s been given since making his senior international debut in last week’s 4-1 win over Peru, scoring it that game shortly after entering as a second half substitute and then finding the net again in his first start, a 4-2 victory against Chile. Those goals were enough for Poch to keep the Manhattan-born Hall in his lineup for Saturday’s showdown with Mexico, the highest-profile match among the four the No. 16-ranked U.S. team will play this window. And Hall rose to the challenge again, giving the home team a 1-0 lead following one of the only extended spells of possession the USA had during a first half in which El Tri had the ball for more than 60 percent of the time. "I mean, three goals in three games is not bad for a striker, especially in your first three games in the national team," said Gio Reyna, whose cross led to Hall's tap-in. "He sort of has that eye for goal." Like most of the rest of the youngsters who Pochettino handed minutes to this month, Hall will probably return to either the U.S. under-20 national team or the 2028 Olympics-bound U-23s when the more experienced forwards in the player pool inevitably return. But for a country that never seems to have enough pure goalscorers, he’s definitely given Poch and his staff something to think about ahead of next month’s Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals. "It's a fantastic problem for us," the coach told me when I asked if the performances of Hall and the other youngsters might alter thier plans. Once its strongest position by far, the U.S. has had a devil of a time producing elite goalkeepers in recent years. But the 20-year-old Kochen is the country’s best backstop prospect in years, and the fact that Poch started him in a hostile environment in Glendale says plenty about the Barcelona product's potential. That talent was on full display in the 58th minute when, with the U.S. clinging to a 1-0 lead and Mexico knocking on the door, he made an all-world stop on El Tri attacker Roberto Alvarado on the way to a clean sheet: "It's one of the greatest moments of my entire life," a beaming Kochen told me about an hour after the final whistle blew. "I'm super thankful that the coach trusted me with this." It remains to be seen if Kochen will keep his place going forward, stick with the senior team in an understudy role, or if he, like others, will return to the youth ranks. Given his competition, his age, and his status as the American keeper with the highest ceiling, don’t be surprised if it’s the first one. The Americans have another quick turnaround following Saturday’s victory, with just two days between the Mexican match and another rivalry game on Tuesday against Canada and its American coach, Jesse Marsch. "We have Canada in three days," said Reyna, the only U.S. player to start all three games during this camp. "First time I started three games in the week in probably four or five years, so I'm a little bit tired now. But I'll be good for Canada." While the U.S. holds the all-time series lead with a record of 17 wins to 12 losses (along with two draws), it has won just once in the last six meetings between the teams, including the most recent in 2025. Can the Red, White and Blue break another streak of futility against another neighbor in Minnesota?

item.title: Cavan Sullivan And Barcelona Prospect Diego Kochen Start For USA vs. Mexico
item.description: What a way to get your first start for the U.S. men’s national team.
item.content:encoded: STATE FARM STADIUM (Glendale, Ariz.) – What a way to get your first start for the U.S. men’s national team. A week after making his senior international debut in the second half of the USA’s 4-1 win over Peru, 20-year-old Barcelona goalkeeper Diego Kochen was named in coach Mauricio Pochettino's lineup for Saturday’s high-profile exhibition with blood rivals Mexico just outside of Phoenix, where a sellout crowd of 64,000 fans is expected at the home of the NFL’s Arizona Cardinals. Cavan Sullivan, who turned 17 on Monday, is also in Pochettino’s 11 against El Tri. The Philadelphia Union attacker started against Peru — becoming the second-youngest starter in the 113-year history of the U.S. men's program and the fourth-youngest overall — and came in off the bench in the Americans' most recent outing, a 4-2 victory over Chile last Tuesday in St. Louis. Kochen earned the nod over Matt Freese, who was between the posts for all five U.S. games at the 2026 FIFA World Cup. Chris Brady and Brian Schwake are the other two keepers in Pochettino’s current squad. Kochen didn’t allow a goal in his 45 minutes of action against Peru. Brady and Schwake each played a half vs. Chile, surrendering one goal apiece. The Stars and Stripes will close out this extended four-game international window against Canada on Tuesday in St. Paul, Minnesota. Although he didn’t make Pochettino’s World Cup roster, Kochen served as a training keeper during the USA’s pre-tournament training camp. Five-time European champs Barça then sent the South Florida native on loan to Danish club Lyngby for the 2026-27 season. Kochen has one clean sheet in nine Danish Superliga games so far, conceding 16 times in all. Pochettino, the 54-year-old former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain manager, said during Friday’s pre-match press conference that his lineup would contain a mix of experienced players and youngsters. Two-time World Cup veterans Antonee Robinson, Gio Reyna and Tyler Adams — who the Argentine named U.S. captain on the eve of the contest — round out the team, which also includes 2026 World Cup goalscorers Alex Freeman, Sebastian Berhalter and Auston Trusty. Eighteen-year-old Red Bull New York striker Julian Hall, who scored in each of his first two U.S. appearances last month, will lead Pochettino’s front line against Mexico. Saturday’s contest marks the second straight start for Hall.

item.title: England Puts 7 Goals Past Croatia As Kane, Saka, Bellingham All Shine
item.description: Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka have scored two each as England crushed Croatia 7-0 in UEFA Nations League action.
item.content:encoded: Harry Kane and Bukayo Saka scored two each as ruthless England crushed Croatia 7-0 away in the Nations League on Saturday. Ballon d’Or contender Kane extended his national record to 89 international goals. Left winger Anthony Gordon set up Jude Bellingham and grabbed one for himself. Substitute Morgan Rogers completed the rout in Rijeka. "It was very impressive, and we created so many chances. In the first 40 minutes we were so fluid right from the start. It just never stopped," England coach Thomas Tuchel said. "We just kept the pace up and played through the gaps. We were very, very clinical." Later in other League A play, World Cup champion Spain hosted Czechia in Oviedo and looked to make it 40 straight games unbeaten. Switzerland faced Slovenia and Scotland went to North Macedonia in League B matches. England cruises Kane put England ahead in the eighth minute, controlling a pass from Bellingham with the outside of his right foot and then curling the ball into the top left corner. Bellingham poked in Gordon's cross midway through the first half. Gordon stooped to head in Jarell Quansah's right-wing cross and Saka side-footed in England's fourth approaching halftime. After the break, Croatia's defense was sliced open again on a quick break and Elliot Anderson curled in a cross from the right and Kane slid in at the back post for a poacher's finish. "We’re at our best when we’re free, when we’re physically just overpowering," Kane said. "They couldn’t live with our pace, our movement, our runs." More bad defending saw Croatia unable to clear the ball and it ended up at the feet of Kane, who gifted Saka his second in the 68th. Rogers controlled Bellingham’s pass with his heel and slotted in from an angle. The result eclipsed England’s previous highest score against Croatia, 5-1 in World Cup qualifying in 2009 at Wembley. Tuchel’s England moved onto six points from three games. Bad start for Bilić It was another tough match for Croatia coach Slaven Bilić following Tuesday's 4-1 loss in Spain. His side has conceded 12 goals in three matches. Luka Modric started the game in Rijeka but the 41-year-old looked frustrated by his team's sloppy performance.

item.title: Lamine Yamal Scores Golazo And Spain's Unbeaten Streak Continues
item.description: Lamine Yamal has kept up his run of early goals as Spain are now riding a 41-game unbeaten streak.
item.content:encoded: Lamine Yamal kept up his run of early goals in the Nations League when he put Spain ahead with a superb sixth-minute goal against Czechia on Saturday. Spain, winners of this summer's World Cup, have now gone 41 matches without a loss. Spain coach Luis de la Fuente shook his head in admiration and disbelief as Yamal cut inside down the right and unleashed a powerful curling shot with his left foot into the top left corner. Goalkeeper Antonín Kinský could not even get near the ball. This trademark Yamal strike followed the 19-year-old star's second-minute goals against Croatia in a 4-1 win on Tuesday and away to England in a 3-2 victory on Sept. 26. The Ballon d'Or contender has also been in outstanding form for defending La Liga champion Barcelona this season. Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: USA-Mexico Is A Huge Test For New Generation: 'Like A Cup Final'
item.description: The intensity of the USA's game against Mexico figures to be unlike anything any of the newcomers have seen before.
item.content:encoded: TEMPE, Arizona — For any international soccer squad (or really a team in any sport at all), hitting the road for games in inhospitable environments is a fact of life. Home-field advantage is real. The flip side of that fact is that it also holds true for opponents. Being the away team is almost always harder. It sure has been for the U.S. men’s national team against Mexico, its fiercest rival. While the USA has gotten the better of El Tri more often than not over the last quarter-century — including a 2-0 win that sent the Americans to the quarterfinals of the 2002 FIFA World Cup, it still has never won a competitive match south of the border since the neighbors first met in one there almost 80 years ago. Saturday’s exhibition between the U.S. and Mexico just outside of Phoenix is technically a home game for the Stars and Stripes. As a practical matter, it isn’t. The overwhelming majority of the 60,000-plus fans expected at State Farm Stadium in nearby Glendale are sure to be rooting for the visiting team. "It's going to be an adverse crowd, tough conditions to play in," veteran American defender Antonee Robinson said on Thursday. "But that's something we embrace." They should. It’s been almost two years since Mauricio Pochettino’s side last played outside the United States. Because the USA qualified automatically as co-hosts of the 2026 World Cup, it didn’t have to earn its way there by collecting points in hostile regional outposts such as Port-of-Spain or San Pedro Sula or Mexico City. That won’t be the case ahead of the 2030 World Cup. Concacaf’s marathon two-year-long qualifying tournament begins late next year. Saturday’s contest will help prepare the U.S. for what’s coming. "It’s a good opportunity for us to live that experience, of course," Pochettino said during his pre-game press conference, adding that if the composition of the crowd resembles the 2025 Gold Cup final that the U.S. narrowly lost to Mexico in front of an ocean of green jerseys in Houston, it will be like starting the game "down 1-nil." "To play in a difficult atmosphere, I think that for sure is going to help for the future." The U.S. kicked off this new World Cup cycle with impressive multi-goal wins over South American foes Peru and Chile. Pochettino started a number of young players against both. The initial feeling was that he’d opt for more experienced lineups for the final two tests of this extended four-match window. But the youngsters did well enough — the Americans got goals from teenagers Mathis Albert and Justin Ellis and two from Julian Hall — to suggest that they won't be at all overawed if they’re called on against Mexico and/or Canada. After facing El Tri, the U.S. will wrap things up in St. Paul, Minnesota, with another rivalry game against their neighbors in the north. "Tomorrow is going to be similar to Peru or Chile," Pochettino said Friday. "We are going to always try to find a good balance, a mix between experienced players and non-experienced players at the international level." Still, the intensity of the game against El Tri figures to be unlike anything any of the newcomers have seen before. "Dislike, hate. I mean, it's a rivalry," said Tyler Adams, who Pochettino announced will inherit the captain’s armband from the now-retired Tim Ream. "Whenever we play Mexico — whether it's a qualifier, a friendly, Gold Cup, Nations League — it's always seen as a must-win game," Robinson said. "It feels like a cup final, and we get a lot of boys who've never experienced that at this level who’ll get to see it for the first time." Given what we’ve seen from the new generation so far, they’ll likley be up for the challenge. "There's a lot of games where we've played and it's been mostly Mexico fans. Some teams could fold under that pressure," Robibnsion continued. "But I think we like the kind of adversity that comes with that. We love when we score and we're getting beers thrown at us and things like that. "It's a great feeling."
